EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered treatment adoption, implemented with modern TWFE-robust estimators (e.g., Callaway–Sant’Anna 2021 or Sun–Abraham 2020) plus an event-study specification for dynamics.  

Why appropriate:  
• The Report on Carcinogens (RoC) listing dates are externally determined by NTP scientists after years of toxicological research, unrelated to any individual firm’s contemporaneous operating or financial choices.  
• The NOES survey provides a pre-determined cross-section of worker exposure (1981-83). This makes “treated” status a pre-treatment characteristic that interacts with quasi-random timing of chemical listings.  
• No obvious running variable around an arbitrary cutoff (so RDD not natural).  
• No credible instrument is needed because the RoC dates yield plausibly exogenous shocks.  

Hence a staggered DID that compares exposed firms before vs. after the listing to non-exposed firms in the same years is the cleanest identification design. The accompanying event-study checks the parallel-trends assumption and reveals adjustment dynamics.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for firm i in year t if:  
• Its 4-digit SIC industry had documented worker exposure to chemical c in NOES, and  
• Chemical c is first listed in RoC in year τ ≤ t, and  
• The firm has not been treated in any prior year (absorbing treatment).  

Formally: Treat_it = 1[Exposure_i × (t ≥ FirstListing_c)] with Exposure_i measured once (1981-83).  

Control group  
• Firms in industries with NOES-measured exposure to *different* chemicals that are not (yet) listed in the RoC by year t.  
• Plus firms in industries with zero recorded exposures (preferred baseline).  
These groups face the same macro conditions and regulatory environment but no surge in liability risk at time t.  

Treatment timing / event date  
Event date = calendar year when the specific chemical is *first* added to the RoC (publication month is typically December; we code event year = RoC edition year).  

Because multiple chemicals are listed over 1980-2006, firms enter treatment in different calendar years (staggered adoption).  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of RoC listings, outcomes (investment, leverage, payouts, etc.) of exposed and unexposed firms would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Exposure data come from an early-1980s snapshot; at that time no one could know which chemicals would be listed years later. We also include firm and industry-year fixed effects, plus test with pre-treatment leads.  

A2. No differential anticipation: Managers cannot precisely time their policies based on the future listing year. Given 3-7-year NTP review cycles, exact publication timing is hard to forecast, making large anticipatory adjustments unlikely.  

A3. No spillovers/contamination: A chemical’s listing does not directly change liability risk for firms that were not exposed in NOES industries. Although general awareness of occupational hazards may rise, the liability tail is sharply greater for firms with documented exposure (strict-liability workers’ comp plus tort suits). We will test for geographic or supply-chain spillovers.  

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Each firm’s outcomes depend only on its own treatment status. If heightened liability at one firm increases competitive rents for rivals, SUTVA could fail; we address this by using industry-year fixed effects and by re-estimating on a sample of industries with few cross-linkages.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

4. Main Threats and Mitigations  

Threat 1: Differential pre-trends (selection on growth paths).  
Mitigation:  
• Event-study leads (-5 to ‑1 years) must be statistically and economically close to zero.  
• Allow industry-specific linear trends or interact pre-period trends with exposure intensity.  

Threat 2: Measurement error in exposure (NOES may miss small plants; firms may enter/exit industries).  
Mitigation:  
• Use intensity (share of workers exposed) as a continuous treatment and estimate dose-response models.  
• Re-classify treatment when firms change primary 4-digit SICs; drop diversified conglomerates in robustness checks.  

Threat 3: Multiple chemical listings in the same industry → overlapping shocks.  
Mitigation:  
• Define treatment as the *first* time any relevant chemical for a firm is listed (absorbing).  
• Cluster standard errors at the industry × RoC-chemical group level.  
• As robustness, isolate single-chemical industries and replicate.  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

5. R Code Outline (executable)  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
install.packages(c("data.table","fixest","did","ggplot2"))
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(did); library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Load data ----
firm   <- fread("compustat_panel.csv")        # firm-year financials
expos  <- fread("noes_exposure.csv")          # SIC4, chemical_id, exposure_share
roc    <- fread("roc_listing.csv")            # chemical_id, listing_year
gov    <- fread("governance_variables.csv")   # firm-year governance
mna    <- fread("sdc_mna.csv")                # firm-year acquis activity

# ---- 2. Merge & variable construction ----
# a. First listing year per chemical
roc[, first_year := min(listing_year), by = chemical_id]

# b. Firm-level exposure indicator & event year
setkey(expos, chemical_id); setkey(roc, chemical_id)
expos <- expos[roc, nomatch = 0]

# Choose largest exposure_share chemical per SIC4 to define primary exposure
expos_primary <- expos[, .SD[which.max(exposure_share)], by = sic4]

# c. Attach to firm panel
setkey(firm, sic4)
firm <- firm[expos_primary, on = "sic4"]

# d. Treatment timing
firm[, treat_year := fifelse(!is.na(first_year), first_year, Inf)]
firm[, treated := fifelse(year >= treat_year, 1L, 0L)]

# e. Event-time dummies for event study (-5 to 10)
for (k in -5:10){
  firm[, paste0("event_",k) := fifelse(year - treat_year == k, 1L, 0L)]
}

# f. Outcome variables
firm[, ln_capx := log(1 + capx/lag(ppent,1))]
firm[, payout_ratio := (dv + repurchases) / cfo]
firm[, leverage := total_debt / assets]

# ---- 3. Baseline DID (Sun & Abraham, via fixest) ----
# Investment example
baseline <- feols(ln_capx ~ sunab(treat_year, year) | gvkey + year,
                  data = firm[year %between% c(1980,2006)],
                  cluster = ~sic4)
summary(baseline)

# ---- 4. Callaway–Sant'Anna aggregate ATT ----
cs_out <- att_gt(yname = "ln_capx",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "gvkey",
                 gname = "treat_year",
                 data = firm[is.finite(treat_year)],
                 est_method = "dr",
                 control_group = "never_treated")
agg_effect <- aggte(cs_out, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effect)
ggdid(agg_effect)  # plot pre- and post-effects

# ---- 5. Robustness: industry-specific trends ----
robust <- feols(ln_capx ~ sunab(treat_year, year) |
                   gvkey + year + i(sic4, year, ref = 0),
                data = firm,
                cluster = ~sic4)
etable(baseline, robust)

# ---- 6. Additional outcome: probability of diversification M&A ----
firm[, div_mna := as.integer(any(mna$target_sic4 != firm$sic4)), by = .(gvkey, year)]
feols(div_mna ~ treated | gvkey + year, data = firm, family = "binomial",
      cluster = ~sic4)
```

──────────────────────────────────────────  

6. Expected Results  

Theory suggests managers will respond to a spike in expected tort liabilities by:  
• Conserving internal cash and reducing discretionary payouts.  
• Lowering leverage to avoid compounding distress risk.  
• Shifting investment from specialized, difficult-to-redeploy assets toward diversified acquisitions that hedge cash-flow volatility.  

Magnitude priors (order of magnitude, not exact):  
• CAPEX within core SIC falls 5-8 % of beginning-of-year PPE over the five years post-listing.  
• Net leverage ratio declines 2–3 p.p. of assets.  
• Payout ratio drops 15–20 %.  
• Probability of a diversifying acquisition rises by ~4 p.p. (baseline mean ≈ 9 %).  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1: No pre-trends (lead coefficients ≈ 0) ………… 1  
C2: Treatment exogeneity / shock plausibly random … 1  
C3: No anticipation / timing manipulation ………… 0.5 (some lobbying possible)  
C4: No spillovers / SUTVA …………………………… 0.5  
C5: Correct inference (clustering, staggered estimator) … 1  

Overall score: 4 / 5 → design appears credible but must validate C3–C4 empirically.
